facebook.long_form:
With 35 games left in the regular season, it's time to talk about what Pete Crow-Armstrong is actually doing in this MVP race — and why the history he's making matters.

PCA right now: .281 batting average. 30 home runs. 78 RBI. 31 stolen bases. 7.7 WAR.

His closest competitor? Shohei Ohtani at approximately 6.4 WAR.

PCA leads in WAR. PCA's team is in first place in the NL Wild Card race. And PCA is on pace for something no Cubs player has ever done: back-to-back 30-30 seasons. Not just once — he already did it last year. He's now on the verge of doing it again. That's never happened in Cubs history.

The argument against him? Name. Ohtani's 2023 MVP win set the bar for name-recognition-driven voting. But the voters who actually look at the numbers, look at the WAR, look at the team standings impact — those voters are going to have a very hard time putting anyone ahead of PCA in 2026.

35 games. The story isn't over. It's just entering the best part. 🐻

stories.title: Joshua Baez Returns from Day Off — Cardinals' Deployment Decision Looms
stories.angle: After his day off Aug 19, Baez is back in the Cardinals lineup and the deployment question has only gotten more interesting. Manager Oliver Marmol has already experimented with the leadoff slot. Baez's numbers (.251/.332/.552, 12 HR in early innings) suggest a middle-order power bat. But his youth, athleticism, and speed complicate the picture. The Cardinals need to decide now whether to commit to a role — and the wrong choice could cost them games in August.

x_posts.label: Post 2
x_posts.text: Joshua Baez is back after his day off. The deployment question: leadoff experiment or cleanup power threat? .251/.332/.552 with 12 HRs says middle order. But Marmol already tried him leadoff. The chess match continues. #Cardinals #STLCards

facebook.long_form:
Joshua Baez is back in the Cardinals lineup after Thursday's rest — and Oliver Marmol still has a decision to make.

What's the right role for a 21-year-old who hit three home runs in his first three career at-bats? Who posted a 449-foot blast on his first MLB swing? Who is batting .251/.332/.552 with 12 home runs in his young career?

Here's the tension:

The .552 slugging percentage says cleanup hitter. Put this bat in the middle of the order where it can do the most damage. Don't waste a plus-plus power threat at leadoff.

But Marmol has already tried him there. He moved Baez to leadoff while resting JJ Wetherholt, giving the young outfielder a look at the top of the lineup. It didn't stick — but the experiment told us something. Marmol is actively figuring this out.

The 32.7% strikeout rate is the number that makes the leadoff case harder. Elite leadoff hitters take pitches. They work counts. They get on base above their batting average. Baez is capable of all of that — but not consistently yet, not with 12 career homers under his belt.

The Cardinals have 35 games left to get this right. With Baez, getting it right could change everything. 🔴

stories.title: Alvarez Triple Crown Math — 35 Games, Three Categories, One Mission
stories.angle: With 35 games remaining and a Triple Crown within range, the math gets specific. Alvarez leads BA (.329) by 29 points — comfortable but not comfortable enough to coast. He trails Schwarber in HRs (36 vs. 37 for Schwarber). He leads RBI substantially (88). What does he need per week, per series, to emerge with all three categories? And how does the August schedule favor or hurt his chances?

x_posts.label: Post 3
x_posts.text: Yordan Alvarez Triple Crown math with 35 games left: BA — leads by ~29 points (comfortable). RBI — leads by a wide margin (comfortable). HR — down 1 to Schwarber at 37. The home run is all that stands between Alvarez and history. Last TC: Cabrera 2012. #Astros #TripleCrown

facebook.long_form:
Yordan Alvarez is 35 games away from the rarest individual accomplishment in baseball.

The last Triple Crown winner was Miguel Cabrera in 2012 — 14 years ago. No one has led the league in batting average, home runs, and RBI simultaneously since then.

Here's where Alvarez stands:

Batting Average: .329. He leads the AL by approximately 29 points. This is the most comfortable of the three categories — a lead that would require a significant cold stretch to lose in 35 games.

Home Runs: 36. Kyle Schwarber has 37 — one ahead. This is the tightest category and the hardest to project. Both hitters can go on a streak. Both can go cold. Alvarez needs to stay hot while Schwarber cools.

RBI: 88. Alvarez leads by a comfortable margin. The Astros are still playing meaningful games, and Alvarez will see RBI opportunities. This category is his to keep.

The math says: keep the BA where it is, hit 5-8 more home runs, and he's there. That's not a certainty — but it's not a fantasy either. The player who last won a Triple Crown did it in the modern era. Alvarez is right there. ⚾

facebook.long_form:
Jacob Misiorowski is pitching the best season in baseball. That sentence isn't hyperbole. Look at the numbers.

12-5 record. 1.76 ERA. 204+ strikeouts. 0.73 WHIP. NL Cy Young odds: -550.

-550 is not a close race. -550 means the market has decided. The only thing that stops Misiorowski from picking up that trophy in November is an injury or an implosion — and this season has shown no signs of either.

His next start comes around August 23, after the Brewers gave him an extra day of rest following the historic 22-0 win over Seattle. The Brewers (78-48) have the best record in baseball, and Misiorowski is the engine of that pitching staff.

What a dominant final stretch looks like: six to eight starts, 40+ innings pitched, ERA staying south of 2.00, strikeout total pushing toward 220. If he does that, the conversation is not whether he wins the Cy Young. It's whether this becomes one of the top 10 pitching seasons of the modern era.

Stay healthy. Keep throwing. The trophy is already in his name. 🍺

facebook.long_form:
The NL Wild Card race has 35 games left, and the Cubs are sitting in the driver's seat.

Here's the standings:
• Cubs: 73-53 (NL Wild Card No. 1)
• Phillies: 68-58 (5 games back)
• Padres: 67-59 (6 games back)

Three Wild Card spots are available in the current playoff format. By the raw standings, all three of these teams could theoretically get in — which is what makes the seeding battle so critical right now.

Specifically: the Cubs want seed No. 1 in the NL Wild Card bracket, because seed No. 1 avoids the Brewers (78-48) in the first round. Playing a team with the best record in baseball at American Family Field is nobody's dream October matchup. Every game down the stretch isn't just about staying in — it's about avoiding that bracket.

The Phillies and Padres see this differently. For them, the priority is simply getting in. Worry about the Brewers later.

35 games left. The NL Wild Card race is alive, it's tight, and the seeding implications are enormous. 🐻⚾
